newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS - Dollar climbs to fresh highs in Europe.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Dollar climbs to fresh highs in Europe.

text.p: The dollar climbed to new multi-year highs against the mark, yen and Swiss franc in European trade on Monday, with little seen standing in its way except the need for some retracement after its strong rally.
Breaching key hurdles at 1.6300 marks and 118 yen, it pushed up persistently to its strongest level against the mark for 31 months and to its highest versus the yen since March 1993.

"It's very well bid today... mainly on the back of mark selling against other European currencies. I suppose we'll see some correction but it's just not a very good idea to sell dollars at the moment," said a trader at a U.S. bank in London.
At the European midsession the dollar was at 1.6308 marks, just off its high of 1.6315, its strongest since June 1994, and well above its level of 1.6117 in late European trade on Friday.
It scored a high of 118.18 yen before backing down to 118.00 by early afternoon, while remaining nearly one yen higher than at the end of last week.

The dollar's strength across the board also took it to 1.4205 Swiss francs, its highest level against the currency since June 1994. It cooled in the afternoon to 1.4125 but was still stronger than Friday's late 1.3938/48.

Expectations that economic growth in the last quarter of 1996 was healthy and other rosy fundamentals for the United States meant there was little to stop the dollar from stretching for new heights, analysts said.
"Both the German and Japanese economies are perceived to be very weak. The U.S. economy by contrast is perceived as very robust," said David Coleman, chief economist at CIBC Wood Gundy.

"Sentiment at the moment is very pro-dollar, anti-mark and anti-yen and it's difficult to see what in the short term will change that, although there will be the odd retracement... You need a very specific reason at the moment to be bearish on the dollar," Coleman said.
A sharp drop in the Tokyo stock market's key Nikkei average, which fell by 3.37 percent overnight, had given the dollar more momentum, traders said.

The currency market was waiting for the release of German M3 money supply data, a key indicator used by the Bundesbank in deciding its money policy. M3 for December was forecast to show growth of 7.5 percent after an 8.0 percent rise the previous month.
Although traders said the market would be watching the M3 figures, few thought the data would have a tremendous impact on the market.

"The Bundesbank is not overly concerned with where the mark is against the dollar. It's more concerned with mark crosses in Europe as a lot of currencies trading strongly against the mark would slightly undermine the mark's reserve currency status," said Bankers Trust international economist Ian Amstad.
"But because of the strong disinflationary forces within the domestic economy, the Bundesbank doesn't have a problem with dollar/mark at 1.62," he said.

The mark continued to slip against other European currencies. It sank to a 31-month low against the lira at 966.45, trading at 968.37 lire in early afternoon, down from its late Friday level of 970.85.

The Norwegian crown and Finnish markka also surged against the mark to their strongest levels since September 1992. Norway's crown was up at 3.9105 per mark from Friday's 3.9365, while the markka was at 2.9125, up from 2.9640.
